title: Return to sender: Lawmakers unhappy with $1,000 checks left on their desks
summary: The many possible reactions to being handed a $1,000 check out of the blue do not often include anger. But that was the case Tuesday when Del. Christopher Eric Bouchat left checks for a senator and two fellow delegates who have called or him to resign.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 31, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 31, 2026

There are many possible reactions to being handed a $1,000 check out of the blue. Anger is not typically one of them.

But that was the case Tuesday when Del. Christopher Eric Bouchat (R-Frederick and Carroll) left checks for the senator and two fellow delegates in his district.

Bouchat said the checks were a gift for his colleagues to donate to the charities of their choice. The check recipients, who last week called on Bouchat to resign, saw it differently.

“I view that as bribe-like and find it inappropriate,” said Senate Minority Whip Sen. Justin Ready (R-Frederick and Carroll). “I reported it right away and am returning it voided.”

Ready and Dels. April Rose and Chris Tomlinson, all Republicans from Bouchat’s District 5, said they contacted legislative ethics counsel after they got the checks.

It was the latest in a series of exchanges between Bouchat and legislators from his own party and district after the freshman lawmaker decided he would no longer fully perform his duties as a delegate.

Carroll legislators call for Bouchat’s resignation

Since the end of February, Bouchat has driven to the State House from his district every day to register his attendance in the House. Soon after, he leaves to go back to his Arbutus-based welding business.

When he was told he could not resign his seat on the House Judiciary Committee, he simply stopped attending.

He wrote to House Minority Leader Del. Jason C. Buckel (R-Allegany) calling on all House Republicans to do the same, to register their anger and frustration at the futility of being a member of the minority party in the heavily Democratic legislature.

Instead, Rose, Tomlinson and Ready signed a letter calling on Bouchat to resign. Bouchat took it in stride, offering to donate some of his salary to charities of his colleague’s choosing.

With Tuesday’s check drop, Bouchat made good on that proposal.

The checks were left in Easter cards on the lawmakers’ desks. The checks, which appeared to be drawn on Bouchat’s personal account, were in the amount of $1,000, with the payee line left blank. In the note section “charitable donation in honor of…” and the name of the lawmaker were written. In the card, Bouchat wrote “Please donate to a local cause in God’s love.”

Tomlinson told a reporter he was advised to “write void on” the check and “mail it back to him with a note saying, ‘No thank you — I don’t find this appropriate,’ and document it.”

Rose said she also was advised to void and return the check.

The advice appears to be more out of an abundance of caution. Gifts between elected officials are not strictly regulated.

In an email Tuesday evening, Bouchat said his offer was sincere, and he called Ready’s use of the word bribe, “a desperate word to use in an attempt to disparage my goodwill towards them.”

Some hoped the House Republican Caucus would discuss changes to its rules that might allow for the removal of a member who refuses to attend sessions and hearings. But internal caucus discussions are considered private, and Buckel brushed off questions about a potential change in caucus rules.

“There is none,” Buckel said when asked of potential rule changes. “There was no discussion.”

When asked how the caucus would deal with a member who decided not to perform the duties of the office to which he was elected, Buckel said, “You don’t.”

“It’s the responsibility of the House of Delegates and the responsibility of their own voters,” he said. “Our caucus is not policing our own members. That’s between that member and their voters.”

By law, the House and Senate set the rules for members. The Maryland Constitution includes some guidance for how legislators can be removed including “failure to act.” But no member of the General Assembly has ever been removed for “failure to act.”

Bouchat is not running for reelection. He has said he wants to run for governor in 2030.

In an email, Bouchat accused Republican Caucus leaders of using Tomlinson against him in a public pressure campaign.

“I do not appreciate what you all do to my friend Chris Tomlinson being a small vulnerable man,” Bouchat wrote in a March 27 email. “You exploit him to be your b–ch and it is a statement about your characters as men.”

“If we were in prison you would be sexually abusing him,” he continued. “If you have issues with my intelligence confront me on my plain (sic). Stop using Chris.”

In his email Tuesday night, Bouchat did not apologize for his language, saying it was “very forceful for a reason.”

“Chris is a friend and I do not appreciate how leadership uses him,” his email said. “It is what is wrong about this political arena.”

Except that Tomlinson said nobody’s using him.

“Bouchat believes that I was forced to sign the letter that asked for him to resign,” Tomlinson said. “Buckel had nothing to do with it. Buckel hasn’t asked for Bouchat’s resignation.”

Buckel was dismissive of Bouchat’s email.

“I have no idea what Bouchat is thinking,” Buckel said. “His emails are foolish and inappropriate and we certainly viewed them as such.”

Tomlinson, in a text with a reporter, said he was offended.

“I do not appreciate his offensive remarks and let me make this clear — I’m nobody’s b–ch.”
